task_spec:
> Using the Global Weather Repository CSV, produce:
> 1. Two ranked bar charts of the **top 10 hottest cities**, one by average and one by single hottest measurement temperature (celsius)
> 2. Two ranked bar charts of the **top 10 hottest countries**, one by average and one by single hottest measurement temperature (celsius)
> 3. **Print the top 10 lists to the console** before plotting: for each of the 4 charts, print the ranked names and their temperature values (e.g., "1. Paris: 25.2 deg C")
> 4. A **100-word summary** for a non-technical audience explaining the rankings and any notable patterns
>
> Column reference: cities are in `location_name`, countries in `country`, temperature in `temperature_celsius`.

report_draft: The world's hottest cities and countries reveal striking contrasts between consistent heat and extreme outliers. Ar Riyadh (Saudi Arabia) and Kuwait top the average-temperature rankings, consistently reaching 45°C and 44.4°C respectively—evidence of sustained desert heat. However, Suva (Fiji Islands) holds the single hottest reading ever recorded: a dramatic 79.3°C, far exceeding any other location. Middle Eastern cities lead the average lists, though Southeast Asian cities like Bangkok and Phnom Penh also rank highly. Doha, Abu Dhabi, and Muscat rank high in both average and extreme-heat lists, showing both steady warmth and occasional extremes. Yet these tropical cities lack the temperature volatility of arid zones, never cracking the top 10 for single hottest readings. The data reveals two different kinds of "hottest": relentless, predictable heat versus rare, spectacular spikes.
